findings.explanation: high confidence.  Witness: The error of the shortest path on the perturbed graph can be as large as Omega(t/epsilon) because the path that minimizes the perturbed distance depends on the noise, so the noise terms along the chosen path are not independent of the path selection. Lemma 2.4 cannot be applied to an adaptively/minimally chosen path without a union bound over all paths of length <= t (of which there can be exponentially many). For instance, in a graph with many paths of hop length t between u and v, taking the minimum noisy path length over-optimizes negative noise, leading to an additive error of Omega(t/epsilon) rather than O(sqrt(t)/epsilon). Previous works [Sea16, CGK+23] achieve O(t/epsilon) precisely because bounding the error uniformly across all paths requires bounding the maximum noise per edge, giving t * max_e |Y_e| = O(t log(n)/epsilon). Consequently, the claimed O(n^{1/3}/epsilon) bound in Theorem 3.1, which relies on Lemma 3.1 with error O(sqrt(t)/epsilon), is incorrect and reverts to O(n^{2/3}/epsilon). We rate our confidence as high because this is a fundamental and well-known fallacy in analyzing input perturbation for shortest paths; the author's argument explicitly asserts that the total error is simply the sum of at most t independent Laplace variables, ignoring the dependency introduced by taking the shortest path on the noisy graph. As a concrete counterexample, let G be a graph with vertices u, v and 2^t edge-disjoint paths of length t between u and v, all with true edge weights 0. Then d_G^{(t)}(u, v) = 0. For each path P_i (i = 1, ..., 2^t), its perturbed length is S_i = sum_{e in P_i} Y_e, where S_i is the sum of t i.i.d. Lap(1/epsilon) variables. The noisy shortest path distance is min_{i} S_i. Since there are 2^t i.i.d. copies of S_i, each having standard deviation Theta(sqrt(t)/epsilon) and exponential-type tails (or even by considering that each edge has probability 1/4 of having noise < -1/epsilon, so with high probability at least one path has all t edges with noise < -1/epsilon, giving sum < -t/epsilon), the expected minimum noisy distance is -Omega(t/epsilon). Thus, |d~^{(t)}(u,v) - d_G^{(t)}(u,v)| = Omega(t/epsilon) with high probability, directly contradicting the claimed O(sqrt(t)/epsilon) bound of Lemma 3.1. Since Lemma 3.1 is invalid, Theorem 3.1 fails as well. This completes the refutation of Theorem 3.1 and Lemma 3.1. Location: Lemma 3.1, proof paragraph 2 (sentence p7-2).
